content.content:
Push to a Git remote

By default, pushes tracking bookmarks pointing to `remote_bookmarks(remote=<remote>)..@`. Use
`--bookmark` to push specific bookmarks. Use `--all` to push all bookmarks. Use `--change` to
generate bookmark names based on the change IDs of specific commits.

When pushing a bookmark, the command pushes all commits in the range from the remote's current
position up to and including the bookmark's target commit. Any descendant commits beyond the
bookmark are not pushed.

If the local bookmark has changed from the last fetch, push will update the remote bookmark to the
new position after passing safety checks. This is similar to `git push --force-with-lease` - the
remote is updated only if its current state matches what Jujutsu last fetched.

Unlike in Git, the remote to push to is not derived from the tracked remote bookmarks. Use
`--remote` to select the remote Git repository by name. There is no option to push to multiple
remotes.

Before the command actually moves, creates, or deletes a remote bookmark, it makes several [safety
checks]. If there is a problem, you may need to run `jj git fetch --remote <remote name>` and/or
resolve some [bookmark conflicts].

[safety checks]: https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/bookmarks/#pushing-bookmarks-safety-checks

[bookmark conflicts]: https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/bookmarks/#conflicts

Usage: jj git push [OPTIONS]

Options:
      --remote <REMOTE>
          The remote to push to (only named remotes are supported)
          
          This defaults to the `git.push` setting. If that is not configured, and if there are
          multiple remotes, the remote named "origin" will be used.

  -b, --bookmark <BOOKMARK>
          Push only this bookmark, or bookmarks matching a pattern (can be repeated)
          
          If a bookmark isn't tracking anything yet, the remote bookmark will be tracked
          automatically.
          
          By default, the specified pattern matches bookmark names with glob syntax. You can also
          use other [string pattern syntax].
          
          [string pattern syntax]: https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/revsets/#string-patterns

      --all
          Push all bookmarks (including new bookmarks)

      --tracked
          Push all tracked bookmarks
          
          This usually means that the bookmark was already pushed to or fetched from the [relevant
          remote].
          
          [relevant remote]: https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/bookmarks#remotes-and-tracked-bookmarks

      --deleted
          Push all deleted bookmarks

content.text:
## On `--deleted`

`jj git push --help` on this version says plainly: "Push all deleted bookmarks." So it is unscoped by design. That is exactly its appeal and exactly its problem.

**What it buys**: one command that does not need the bookmark name typed a second time, and it sweeps up any earlier cycle that deleted a bookmark locally and never published the deletion. Given this repo has six cycles' worth of history on one bookmark and a `punctuation-sweep` and `ffq-spsc-notes` still lying around, there may well be such residue.

**Why I would still not put it in the land recipe**: it publishes whatever pending deletions happen to exist, not the one you just made. Deleting a remote ref is outward-facing and awkward to undo, and this is the same class of hazard as `git push --all`, where the blast radius is the repo's ambient state rather than the action you took. The scoped form says what it will do before it does it; `--deleted` requires you to go inspect state first to know, which means the safe way to use it involves a step the convenience was supposed to save.

There is also a cleanliness argument. Sweeping stale remote refs is maintenance, and landing a cycle is a cycle step. Bundling them means an unrelated bookmark can vanish during a close-out, and that deletion lands in no record, since the cycle's records describe the cycle.

**Where it does belong**: as a deliberate sweep of its own, run when you mean it, ideally after listing what is pending. That is a real chore and this repo probably needs one.

## Which is the better answer to both of your points at once

A `vc-x1 land <bookmark>` can have it both ways: do the scoped deletion, and *report* any other locally-deleted-but-unpushed bookmarks without touching them. The sweep becomes visible without becoming automatic, which is the property `--deleted` cannot give you on its own.

What I would ask them for, and I agree it belongs in the message:

- **Preconditions it enforces**: the bookmark is a descendant of the permanent branch, refused outright rather than offered a flag, since `jj.md` already says needing `--allow-backwards` wants a look and not a flag.
- **What it does**: move the permanent branch, push it, delete the bookmark locally and remotely. Work repo only, since the bot repo has no bookmark and its `main` rides the tip.
- **What it reports without doing**: that the as-built backfill is now due, landing being its trigger and that trigger currently having no enforcement anywhere, and any other pending deletions.
- **Approval**: interactive by default like `vc-x1 push`, because it is the moment a cycle's history becomes permanent, which is the single least reversible thing we do.
- **What it must not do**: check the project's records. `vc-x1 push` deliberately assumes nothing about a repo beyond `.jj` and `.vc-config.toml`, and a land command that verified the chores section existed would break that principle. It reminds; it does not inspect.

It also completes the set they have already half-designed. `jj.md` says a `vc-x1 start-change <bookmark>` will eventually own the create half, and the reason the rule and the commands are separated in that file is precisely so a tool can take the commands later. `start-change` / `push` / `land` is the whole cycle, and land is the only one still hand-run.

The plain version: `--deleted` is handier but unscoped, so I would keep the named form in the recipe and treat `--deleted` as its own deliberate cleanup. And yes, ask vc-x1 for `land`, which can report the stale ones instead of silently publishing their deletion.

## What is actually dangling

Not the landing. `main` moving is recorded in jj and git history perfectly well. What has no anchor is the *reasoning*. `ochid:` is a commit-to-commit link, so a beat that produces no work-repo commit has nothing to link from. When the next `vc-x1 push` runs, this transcript gets swept into that push's bot commit, whose trailer will name a work commit about something else entirely. The session that decided to land, and that produced two family findings, gets filed under an unrelated title.

Landing is not the only beat with no work commit. **Writing the message to vc-x1 is another, and it is sharper**: the message goes into the template repo, produces no work-repo commit at all, and generates a lot of reasoning. Worse, vc-x1 warned that the template repo has no commits, so nothing archives the message itself. The reasoning behind it would live only in a bot commit linked to something unrelated, and the message it explains would live only in an uncommitted working copy. That is the same hole twice over, on the very next task.

Landing has a natural anchor and it is already owed: **the as-built backfill**. Those ten rungs take their SHAs *because* of the landing, so the backfill commit is the work-repo artifact of this beat. If the backfill is the next thing we push, this transcript is swept into that commit's bot commit and the link reads correctly, the session that landed filed under the commit that records the landing. That is my recommendation for the immediate next step, ahead of the message.

- **Land commits and pushes the bot repo**, so the session that made history permanent is itself published rather than left uncommitted. That alone closes most of the gap.
- **The trailer can only go one way, and the tool should say so.** With no new work commit, the meaningful stamp is the landed tip: a bot commit whose `ochid:` names the commit that became permanent. The reverse link cannot exist, because that work commit is already published and hard rule 4 forbids re-describing it to add a trailer. - The rung form is `- [[N]] [<title>][M]` while the commit is unlanded, becoming
  `- [[2]] X.Y.Z[-n] [<title>][M]` at backfill, as the first rung above shows. `[M]` is the
  rung's subsection link, a file-local slot defined as a same-file fragment
  (`[M]: #<slug>`): it rides in from the working ladder and stays valid, since the
  subsections move into the same file, renumbered like any other slot (the closing rung is
  unlinked unless close-out gotchas gave it a subsection). No step number and no
  `(current)` / `(done)` marker,
  since as-built implies done (the in-flight markers live in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`).
  Landing order is the list order. See
  [Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered).
- **The version arrives with the SHA, not before it.** It is the one version written into prose
  (see
  [Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)),
  because here it records what a landed commit carried rather than naming a step, and together
  with the SHA it decodes an old `-V` banner. On an unlanded branch it is as rewritable as the
  SHA, so it waits for the same moment (Timing, below). The version is knowable earlier, from the
  manifest. Holding it back is deliberate, buying one timing rule and a record a rebase cannot
  falsify.
- Two headers in one chores file must not share a title, or their anchors collide and the
  duplicate silently resolves to the first. Within a file that is the whole uniqueness
  requirement. Titles may repeat across the repo's history.
- A rung is written with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and backfilled in place with a real
  file-local slot once its commit's SHA is permanent (see Timing below).
- Rung citations use the file-local `[N]` reference machinery (see
  [Reference numbering](#reference-numbering)), **double-bracketed** so the brackets render.
  (`[[3]]` shows as a literal `[`, the `[3]` link, then a literal `]`; the inner `[3]`
  resolves against its `[3]:` definition, and CommonMark / GitHub / VS Code all do this.) The
  `# References` definition puts the **commit URL** as the destination, with the **full
  40-hex SHA** in the title slot:

```
[3]: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/commit/<12-hex> "<40-hex>"
```

- The 12-hex short SHA in the URL keeps it short, and GitHub / GitLab resolve a unique prefix to
  the canonical commit page (GitLab's path has a `/-/` before `commit/`).
- The full SHA in the title is host-agnostic and unambiguous: it survives a repo host change,
  `git show <40-hex>` works in any clone, and external tooling scraping the notes (a database,
  say) gets the canonical identifier.

**Timing.** A commit's SHA isn't stable until it lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a
long-lived release/patch branch), because a rebase or squash rewrites it on the way, and neither
is its version. A commit can't record its own SHA, so the fill lands one push later: every rung

## chore: sync cycle records and mailbox sweep

- [[16]] 0.24.6 chore: sync cycle records and mailbox sweep

A single-commit cycle whose entire product is another cycle's record, which is why it went a day
without one of its own. Written after the fact, on 2026-08-12, from the commit and the session it
was pushed from.

### Problem

The sync cycle landed with its chores section unwritten, and the mailbox sweep it triggered had
no durable record at all, which the messaging rule forbids: a message can never be a record, so
anything in one worth keeping is copied out before the entry is deleted.

### Solution

Write the sync cycle's section, carve the commit-body form proposal out as its own anchored
subsection so a message can point at it, and record the sweep, naming what was deleted and what
was copied out first.

### Acceptance check

Nothing deleted from the mailbox that morning survives only in the mailbox.

**Result: passed**, 2026-08-12. The deleted entries' durable content is the residue decoder and
the `vc-x1-dev` switch, both in the sync section's
[Mailbox sweep](#mailbox-sweep-2026-08-12). Everything else in them was already recorded on
vc-x1's side and remains reachable through the standing 2026-08-08 message, which was not
deleted.

### Ladder

- [[16]] chore: sync cycle records and mailbox sweep

### Deliberation

**Why it had no section of its own until now.** Its work was writing another cycle's record, so
its output lives inside the section above rather than beside it, and the close-out that would have
noticed was the same close-out being repaired. That is the shape of the whole debt this cycle
clears: a records commit is the one kind of commit whose own records are easiest to forget.

## chore: complete the landed records

- [[N]] chore: complete the landed records

A single-commit cycle run immediately after `main` moved to the `agent-files-model` tip, because
landing is the beat that makes the records below both possible and due.

### Problem

Eight commits became permanent at once and their records were incomplete in three ways: seven
as-built ladders still held literal `[[N]]` placeholders, waiting on exactly the permanence that
had just arrived; the records cycle at 0.24.6 had no chores section at all; and `## Done` was
missing the entries for 0.24.5 and 0.24.6, so the list of what shipped did not list two things
that had.

### Solution

Backfill the as-built ladders with the SHAs and versions the landing made stable, write the
missing section, and write the two missing `## Done` entries.

### Acceptance check

No `[[N]]` placeholder remains on a landed commit's rung, every landed commit has a chores
section and a `## Done` entry, and every rung citation resolves to a definition in
`# References`.

**Result: passed**, 2026-08-12. The only `[[N]]` left in the file is this cycle's own rung, which
is unlanded and correct to leave, plus one inside a prose sentence quoting the placeholder form.

### Ladder

- [[N]] chore: complete the landed records

### Deliberation

**Why now rather than at leisure.** The backfill was owed the moment `main` moved, and doing it
immediately gave this session's reasoning a home. Landing produces no work-repo commit, so the
conversation that decided to land, and that produced the duplication finding and the
`vc-x1 land` design, had nothing to hang an `ochid:` trailer from and would otherwise have been
swept into the next unrelated commit's session (wink's observation). The backfill is the
work-repo artifact of the landing beat, so filing that session under it is not a convenience, it
is the correct home.

**The version rides with the SHA, and only on the as-built rung.** Hard rule 9 keeps versions out
of ladder prose; the as-built rung is the one named exception, since it records what a landed
commit carried and, beside the SHA, decodes an old `-V` banner. So the six-item `### Ladder`
rungs took their citations and no version.

**A duplication noticed while doing it, not fixed here.** In a single-step cycle the as-built
ladder and the six-item `### Ladder` are the same one rung written twice, which is the same
disease as the checklist and the protocol holding the same nine steps. Recorded for the
duplication cycle rather than solved mid-backfill.

| After the final push | After push or squash-push: stop and wait |

nine steps in the same order, differing only in wordiness.

checklist's own header says the protocol wins on any disagreement. So the file an agent is
instructed to read at the moment of action is, by construction, the copy that loses. Every drift

rung written twice. If the structure produces this from an agent actively thinking about
duplication, it will produce it reliably from one who is not.

numbered imperatives and owns them. The protocol stops restating the steps and holds what a
checklist cannot: the reasoning, the recovery procedures, the close-out shapes, the trapezoid
recipe. It refers to steps by name rather than by number, so renumbering cannot desynchronize
them.

instrument is a real need. This does not undo the split. It makes the checklist authoritative for
the steps it lists, which is what makes it safe to read alone.

form taken from you as-is with nothing we differ on, and validation required at every commit,

already in force here, so diff against our `main` rather than a bookmark.

Still owed, in the full reply: our formal review of your set, our answer on whether a notes entry
stays a numbered list item, a tooling ask, and a naming objection of wink's. None of those is
time-sensitive; this is.

Done when: you have said whether you read the duplication the same way, and if so whether the
direction above is the one you want, the remedy being as much yours to shape as ours.

vc-x1-dev 0.78.8-8

Commit both repos, push the work repo's BOOKMARK, and
squash-push the bot repo's `main`: one command.

Collapses the manual commit-push-publish ceremony into a
single subcommand with two interactive approval gates.

Stages, in order:
  - review           approve the diff (first gate)
  - message          $EDITOR, or --title/--body; approve
                     the text (second gate). Skipped when
                     neither repo has pending changes
  - commit-work      commit the work repo. Skipped when
                     `@` is empty
  - commit-bot       commit `.claude`. Skipped when it is
                     clean
  - bookmark-set     work repo -> <bookmark>, bot -> main
  - push-work        publish <bookmark> to origin
  - squash-push-bot  fold `.claude`'s trailing writes
                     into its commit and push main

Rerunning is always safe: each stage does nothing when its
work is already done, so a failed run is re-run rather than
resumed. There is no saved state: vc-x1 cannot know why a
run failed, so it stops and reports. Please fix and try
again.

Failures in commit-work / commit-bot / bookmark-set roll both
repos back via `jj op restore` to a snapshot taken moments
earlier. Once push-work succeeds the work is published: from
there a change is either a new commit appended on top by the
next push, or an amend of what was pushed: `vc-x1
squash-push` folds the working copy into the last commit and
force-updates the remote.

vc-x1 runs no build or test steps: run your project's checks
yourself before pushing.

Non-interactive use: pass both --title and --body plus --yes
to skip both gates.

Usage: vc-x1-dev push [OPTIONS] [BOOKMARK]

Arguments:
  [BOOKMARK]
          Bookmark to advance in the work repo (positional form of
          `--bookmark`). The bot repo always advances `main`.
          
          Accepting a positional lets the common case read as `vc-x1 push main`
          without the `--bookmark` ceremony; `--bookmark` is kept as an alias
          for scripts and for composition with other args. The two forms
          conflict if both supplied.

Options:
      --bookmark <BOOKMARK>
          Bookmark to advance in the work repo (flag form; see positional)

  -V, --version...
          Version detail on stdout: -V the banner, -VV the full report (as
          `vc-x1 version`). Counted like -v/-vv.
          
          Both ride along: they print, then the subcommand runs, so one
          invocation captures the version and the command's output together.
          That is why this replaces clap's auto-version, which would exit after
          printing. Without either, the banner still prints, on stderr.

      --no-banner
          Suppress the banner stderr normally carries on every run.
          
          Only the ambient banner: an explicit `-V` still prints, since asking
          for it outranks suppressing it.

      --step
          Pause between every stage for an interactive approval gate

      --allow-jj-mismatch
          Run even when `jj -V` disagrees with our linked jj-lib.
          
          Per-invocation on purpose, never a config key: a key gets set once
          during a frustrating afternoon and then silently protects nothing.

      --no-squash-push
          Stop before `squash-push-bot` so it can be run manually

      --dry-run
          Print the exact commands for every stage without side effects

  -v, --verbose...
          Verbose output: -v debug, -vv trace

      --log <LOG>
          Log file path (captures all levels)

      --title <STR>
          Commit title (skip `$EDITOR` for the message stage)

      --body <STR>
          Commit body (skip `$EDITOR` for the message stage)

  -y, --yes
          Auto-approve interactive prompts (review gate, message-edit
          confirmation). Required when `--title` / `--body` aren't both supplied
          in non-interactive contexts

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

```
push bookmark-set: bookmark set chore-complete-the-landed-records -r @- -R .

"Advance" is `jj bookmark set <bookmark> -r @-`, a pointer move onto the commit the push just created. No merge, no integration of two lines, no merge commit. It is a fast-forward only in the trivial sense that the new position is a descendant of the old, because push appended that commit itself a moment earlier.

Which raises something worth checking, because it bears directly on the `vc-x1 land` ask: **landing uses the same primitive**. I ran `jj bookmark set main -r <bookmark>`, which is the same operation over a longer distance. If that is all "advance" means, then `vc-x1 push main` with an empty work `@` may already be most of a land, and it would commit and push the bot repo too, which is the dangling-session gap you spotted. `--dry-run` prints the exact commands with no side effects, so it costs nothing to find out.

content.text:
Measured, and it answers your earlier ochid worry directly.

`vc-x1 push main` with an empty work `@` would run:

```
commit-work      skip (no pending work changes), and it warns:
                 "the supplied message is not applied: the existing
                 top commit is published as-is"
commit-bot       jj commit -R .claude -m "<title>" -m <body+ochid>
bookmark-set     jj bookmark set main -r @- -R .        <- this is the land
push-work        jj git push --bookmark main -R .
squash-push-bot  fold and push .claude main
```

So **landing and advancing are the same primitive**, `jj bookmark set`, and `vc-x1 push main` is the land plus the bot-side commit. Had I run that this afternoon instead of the two raw jj commands, the session would have been committed with an `ochid:` trailer and nothing would have dangled. That is the gap you spotted, and the tool already closes it by accident.

Two things it still does not do, which is precisely the shape of the `land` ask:

- **It does not delete the bookmark**, so the topic-versus-long-lived collision would have persisted.
- **It has no descendancy check of its own.** It sets `main` to `@-` and relies on jj refusing a backwards move. Setting `main` to wherever the working copy happens to sit is a sharper edge than landing a named bookmark, since `@-` is wherever you last were rather than something you named.

And one wrinkle worth naming: with no work changes, the title and body you supply land **only on the bot commit**. You would be authoring a commit message for a work-repo commit that is not created, which reads oddly and means the two histories carry different titles for the same beat.

That reshapes the tooling ask usefully. `vc-x1 land <bookmark>` is not new machinery, it is `push` with the bookmark named instead of `@-`, plus the delete, plus refusing a non-descendant outright, plus a title convention for a bot-only commit. Worth telling them, since "reuse four of your five existing stages" is a much cheaper request than the one I was going to send.

I have added the measurement to the scratch notes so it reaches the message. Nothing was written by the dry run.

message.content:
You "land" means:
- push <current-bookmark> with a description and set ochid
- ff-merge a different bookmark to <current-bookmark>
- delete <current-bookmark>

Is that correct

content.text:
Nearly. Three corrections, one of them substantive.

**Step 1 is right, and bundling it is the good part.** `vc-x1 push <bookmark>` with a description and an ochid is what gives the landing act a record. That is the fix for what we hit today. The wrinkle I measured: if the work repo has no pending changes, `commit-work` is skipped and your description lands only on the bot commit, so you are writing a message for a work commit that does not exist. Land needs a rule for that case, either "the description is bot-only and that is expected" or "land always has something to say in the work repo", and the second is false, since a landing often follows a finished close-out.

**Step 2 is not a merge.** It is `jj bookmark set main -r <bookmark>`, a pointer move. Nothing is combined, no merge commit exists, and the work repo's history is unchanged by it. "Fast-forward" is right as a *constraint*, since it must be refused unless `main` is an ancestor of the bookmark, but "merge" is the wrong verb. I would say **advance the permanent branch to the bookmark**. Also "a different bookmark" understates it: the target is specifically the permanent branch, and that asymmetry is the whole point, since `main` is the thing being made permanent.

**Step 3 is two operations, not one**, and the second is a push: `jj bookmark delete <bookmark>` locally, then `jj git push --bookmark <bookmark>` to publish the deletion. Miss the second and the remote ref survives, which is the stale-bookmark residue we were discussing earlier.

So the corrected definition:

1. `vc-x1 push <bookmark>` with a description, ochid stamped, which records the landing session
2. advance the permanent branch to `<bookmark>`, refused outright if it is not a fast-forward
3. delete `<bookmark>`, locally and remotely

One thing that cannot be inside it: the as-built backfill. Landing is what makes those SHAs stable, so the backfill is necessarily a commit *after* the land, which is why land should report it as due rather than try to do it. That is the one piece of today's sequence the tool can only remind you about.

If that reads right to you, I will put this definition in the message to vc-x1 as the ask, with the measurement that four of its five stages already exist in `push`.

content.text:
Then yes, your model is right and my correction was answering a question you did not ask. At the logical level `git merge --ff-only` is exactly this: main's tip advances to the branch tip, no merge commit, nothing combined. "ff-merge" is the correct name for it, and "pointer move" was me describing the same act one layer down.

So, in git terms, what you wrote is the whole of it:

1. push the branch with its final commit
2. ff-merge main to the branch
3. delete the branch

The only thing I would add is not a correction but a difference in our model: **in plain git there is no step 1**. You would have pushed the branch already, and landing would be steps 2 and 3 alone. Step 1 is in your list because our landing act needs a record of itself, since the reasoning lives in the bot repo and only a commit can carry an `ochid:`. That is dual-repo-specific and it is the reason today's landing left a dangling session.

The one thing worth keeping from the constraint side, also a git-level fact: if it is not a fast-forward, main has moved independently and the situation wants a look rather than a real merge or a rebase chosen automatically. Our rule already says refuse rather than offer a flag.

message.content: I'm not sold on the "land" name yet, but fine as a strawman, and good idea about refusing for now. Would we have two bookmarks for the general case? Maybe --source <SOURCE> and <SOURCE> would default to <current-bookmark> and --target <TARGET> and <TARGET> would default to `main`?

content.text:
Yes, two, and making both explicit-with-defaults is the right shape. Four thoughts on it.

**The target default should come from config, not be hardcoded `main`.** `cycle-checklists.md` already says the permanent branch is whatever the project calls it, so `--target` wants to default to a configured permanent-branch key rather than the literal `main`. That is a new config key, which lands neatly in the `.vc-config.md` schema work they are doing right now, and it means a project on `trunk` or a release branch does not have to pass `--target` on every invocation.

**The source default is the hard one, because jj has no current branch.** Git's "current branch" is a checkout concept that jj deliberately does not have, so "defaults to `<current-bookmark>`" needs a written rule. The honest one is something like: the bookmark pointing at `@` or `@-` that is a descendant of the target, and refuse when zero or more than one match. Worth noting `vc-x1 push` did not attempt this, it made BOOKMARK positional and let you say it. Inferring is friendlier but it is the kind of inference that is right ninety times and then quietly lands the wrong line, so if it infers, it should print what it inferred before acting.

**Transposition is safe by construction, which is a real argument for the two-positional form.** If someone writes the arguments backwards, the command tries to fast-forward the cycle bookmark to `main`, and since `main` is an ancestor of it that is a backwards move, refused by the same rule that refuses a non-fast-forward. So the ff-only constraint you just endorsed also makes the argument order self-checking. That is worth stating in the help text, because it is the sort of property a user will not assume.

**Shape**: `<SOURCE> [TARGET]` positionally with `--source` / `--target` aliases matches what `push` already does, including its "the two forms conflict if both supplied" rule. I would keep that symmetry rather than invent a second convention.

On the name, since you are not sold: the thing I would optimize for is that it says the *whole* act, because merge-and-then-delete is two things and a name that only says the first will surprise. `merge` is what a git user calls step 2 and nothing else, so `vc-x1 merge` that also deletes the source is the most familiar and the most likely to astonish. `advance` is already the family's word for moving a bookmark, in `push`'s own help text, so reusing it here is consistent but collides with what `push` does to the cycle bookmark every commit. If it were mine I would look at `finish`, since finishing a cycle is exactly the act and it implies the cleanup, but I hold that loosely and "land" as a strawman costs nothing until the command exists.

wink's position, verbatim:

> Wink thinks the duplication of the 9 rules is guaranteeing drift in the future and we should
> contemplate eliminating the duplication

**The measurement.** `cycle-checklists.md` has 11 sections and nearly every one has a counterpart
in `cycle-protocol.md`:

| cycle-checklists.md | cycle-protocol.md |
| --- | --- |
| The cycle at a glance | Cycles |
| Cycles run on a bookmark | Topic bookmarks are drafts |
| Opening checklist | Preparation |
| Per-commit checklist, nine steps | Per-commit flow, the same nine steps |
| Ladder (sub-cycle) checklist | Per-Work-commit contract within a ladder |
| Before any push | Pushing / Policy |
| After the final push | After push or squash-push: stop and wait |
| Close-out checklist | Close-out |

`Topic bookmarks are drafts` is a section heading in both files. The per-commit lists are the same
nine steps in the same order, differing only in wordiness.

**The argument we would lead with.** Hard rule 7 says read the checklist before acting. The

## Landing a cycle has no command, and doing it by hand loses the session

We landed `agent-files-model` onto `main` this afternoon with raw jj, and it cost us a record.
Landing produces no work-repo commit, so there was nothing for an `ochid:` trailer to hang from,
and the session that decided to land, and that produced everything in this message, was left
uncommitted in the agent repo with nothing pointing at it. Its natural fate is to be swept into
the next unrelated commit's session. wink's read is that this is a reason to do it with vc-x1
rather than by hand, and we agree.

**Most of it already exists.** `vc-x1-dev push main --dry-run` on an empty work `@` reports:

```
commit-work      skip (no pending work changes)
commit-bot       jj commit -R .claude -m "<title>" -m <body+ochid>
bookmark-set     jj bookmark set main -r @- -R .
push-work        jj git push --bookmark main -R .
squash-push-bot  fold and push .claude main
```

That is the land, plus the agent-repo commit that fixes the lost session. Had we run it instead of
raw jj, nothing would have dangled.

**What it does not do**, and what the command would add:

- **It does not delete the source bookmark.** For us that mattered: `agent-files-model` had hosted
  six cycles without landing, which by `jj.md`'s own text made it a long-lived bookmark and a
  topic bookmark at once, and those are defined as mutually exclusive.
- **It has no descendancy check.** It sets the target to `@-` and leans on jj refusing a backwards
  move. Setting the permanent branch to wherever the working copy happens to sit is sharper than
  advancing it to a bookmark you named.
- **With no work changes, the description lands only on the agent-repo commit.** You author a
  commit message for a work commit that is never created. Whatever the command does here should be
  a stated rule rather than an emergent one.

**The operation, in git terms** (wink's framing, and the right level to design at): push the
branch with its final commit, ff-merge main to the branch, delete the branch. In plain git there
is no first step; it is in ours only because the landing act needs a record of itself.

**Shape we would want:**

- `<SOURCE> [TARGET]` positionally with `--source` / `--target` aliases, matching what `push`
  already does with BOOKMARK, including its rule that the two forms conflict if both are supplied.
- **`--target` defaults to a configured permanent branch, not to the literal `main`.**
  `cycle-checklists.md` already says the permanent branch is whatever the project calls it, so this
  wants a config key, which is a small addition to the schema work you have in flight.
- **`--source` defaulting to "the current bookmark" needs a written rule**, because jj has no
  current branch. Something like the bookmark at `@` or `@-` that descends from the target, and a
  refusal when zero or more than one match. If it infers, it should print what it inferred before
  acting: this is the kind of inference that is right ninety times and then quietly lands the
  wrong line.
- **Refuse a non-fast-forward outright, no override flag.** `jj.md` already says needing
  `--allow-backwards` means the situation wants a look rather than a flag.
- **Transposed arguments are then safe by construction**, which is worth saying in the help text:
  swapping source and target asks to move the cycle bookmark backwards onto the permanent branch,
  which the fast-forward rule refuses.
- **It cannot do the as-built backfill**, since landing is what makes those SHAs stable, so the
  backfill is necessarily the next commit. It should report the backfill as due, and reporting it
  is worth real money: that trigger currently has no enforcement anywhere.
- **It should report other pending bookmark deletions without acting on them.**
  `jj git push --deleted` would publish every pending deletion rather than the one just made,
  which is handier and unscoped; a land command can surface the residue without adopting that
  blast radius.

**The name is unsettled.** "land" is our strawman and wink is not sold. Two related points: a name
that says only the merge will surprise, since the source bookmark also disappears; and separately
wink's judgment that "land it" is too cryptic for the agent-files, where the operation should
probably be spelled out as moving the permanent branch to the bookmark and pushing it. That
affects hard rule 13, `cycle-checklists.md`'s close-out step, and `jj.md`'s section title.

Still owed, in the full reply: our formal review of your set, our answer on whether a notes entry
stays a numbered list item, and one more undocumented convention we tripped over today. None of
those is time-sensitive; these two are.

Done when: you have said whether you read the duplication the same way, and if so whether the
direction above is the one you want, the remedy being as much yours to shape as ours; and whether
the land command is something you want to own, since four of its five stages are already yours.

No, it is not well defined, and the grep makes that concrete. The word appears about thirty times across the pinned set. Exactly one sentence comes close to defining it:

`agent-data/jj.md:133` - **Land**, once the close-out is approved: fast-forward the permanent branch to the bookmark.

Three problems with that being the definition:

- **It lives in the commands file**, under a heading that already assumes the term (`Cycle bookmarks: create and land`). Hard rule 13 uses "lands on it" with no definition and no link, and `cycle-checklists.md` links to jj.md for the *commands*, not for the meaning. So a reader meets the word three times before reaching the one sentence that says what it is, if they ever follow the link.
- **It excludes the deletion.** jj.md's next bullet says the bookmark "is redundant once landed and is deleted", which puts deletion after landing, not inside it. Hard rule 13 reads the same way. So your three-step definition is broader than the written one, and neither of us was wrong, because the text does not say.
- **It says nothing about the final push**, which is the step we established exists only because the landing act needs a record of itself.

And there are **two distinct senses in use**, which nothing distinguishes: a *bookmark* lands, meaning the act of advancing the permanent branch; and a *commit* is *landed*, meaning it now sits on a permanent branch. `prose.md`, `versioning.md`, and `cycle-protocol.md` all use the second sense, including in the as-built rung rule that governed today's backfill.

That reframes the message's last bullet: the problem is not that we lack a good name for a command, it is that the concept is undefined, which is a documentation gap that exists whether or not a command is ever written.

- The draft says the proposal "does not undo the split". You just said you would merge the two files. I would state the range honestly: the minimum is de-duplicating, your inclination is one file, and let them argue the case for two if they have one.

## 2026-08-12 from iiac-perf (o5) + wink: duplicated cycle rules, and a land command

Two items ahead of the full reply, both early on purpose: the first compounds with every commit
you write, the second is a hole we fell into this afternoon.

### Nine steps in two files

wink, verbatim:

> Wink thinks the duplication of the 9 rules is guaranteeing drift in the future and we should
> contemplate eliminating the duplication

* `cycle-checklists.md` has 11 sections and nearly every one restates a `cycle-protocol.md`
  section. The per-commit lists are the same nine steps in the same order, and
  `Topic bookmarks are drafts` is a heading in both files.

  | cycle-checklists.md | cycle-protocol.md |
  | --- | --- |
  | The cycle at a glance | Cycles |
  | Cycles run on a bookmark | Topic bookmarks are drafts |
  | Opening checklist | Preparation |
  | Per-commit checklist, nine steps | Per-commit flow, the same nine steps |
  | Ladder (sub-cycle) checklist | Per-Work-commit contract within a ladder |
  | Before any push | Pushing / Policy |
  | After the final push | After push or squash-push: stop and wait |
  | Close-out checklist | Close-out |

* Hard rule 7 says read the checklist before acting; the checklist's header says the protocol wins
  on any disagreement. The file an agent is told to read at the moment of action is, by
  construction, the copy that loses.
* Today gave three instances: our `custom-family.md` pointed at "step 4" after the sync moved
  validation to step 5; our session wrote one new rule into both files, was corrected by wink, then
  over-corrected; and a single-step cycle's chores as-built ladder and its six-item `### Ladder`
  are the same rung written twice.
  - The checklist keeps the numbered imperatives and owns them. The protocol drops the restatement
    and holds the reasoning, the recovery procedures, the close-out shapes and the trapezoid
    recipe, referring to steps by name so renumbering cannot desynchronize them.
  - This does not undo the split. A fast-read instrument is a real need; making it authoritative
    for what it lists is what makes it safe to read alone.

### Landing a cycle has no command

* We moved `main` with raw jj today and lost a record by it. Landing creates no work-repo commit,
  so nothing carried an `ochid:`, and the session that decided to land was left dangling in the
  agent repo.
  - `vc-x1 push main --dry-run` on an empty work `@` already runs four of the five stages: skip
    commit-work, commit-bot with the ochid, `jj bookmark set main -r @-`, push main, squash-push
    the agent repo. Running that instead would have lost nothing.
* Three gaps remain: it does not delete the source bookmark, it has no descendancy check of its
  own (it sets the target to `@-` and leans on jj refusing a backwards move), and with no work
  changes the description lands only on the agent-repo commit, a message for a work commit that is
  never created.
  - In git terms, wink's framing: push the branch, ff-merge main to it, delete it. The first step
    is ours alone, because our landing act needs a record of itself.
  - `<SOURCE> [TARGET]` positional with `--source` / `--target` aliases, as `push` already does
    with BOOKMARK.
  - `--target` defaults to a configured permanent branch, not the literal `main`:
    `cycle-checklists.md` already says the permanent branch is whatever the project calls it.
  - `--source` defaulting to the current bookmark needs a written rule, jj having no current
    branch, and should print what it inferred before acting.
  - Refuse a non-fast-forward outright, no override flag. Transposed arguments are then safe by
    construction, which is worth stating in the help.
  - It cannot do the as-built backfill, landing being what makes those SHAs stable, so it reports
    the backfill as due. That trigger has no enforcement anywhere today.
  - It reports other pending bookmark deletions without acting on them, where
    `jj git push --deleted` would publish all of them.
* The name is unsettled. "land" is our strawman: a name saying only the merge will surprise, since
  the source bookmark also disappears. Separately, wink judges "land it" too cryptic for the
  agent-files, which affects hard rule 13, the close-out step, and `jj.md`'s section title.

Still owed, in the full reply: our formal review of your set, our answer on whether a notes entry
stays a numbered list item, and one more undocumented convention we tripped over today.

is the one you want; and whether the land command is yours to own, four of its five stages already
being yours.

content.text:
Your framing is the accurate one for what jj does: `jj bookmark set main -r <bookmark>` moves `main`, so `main` is what travels and the bookmark's tip is where it arrives. It also matches the revset you preferred, `main::chore-...`, which reads left to right as from-here-to-there.

The trouble is that git's framing says the exact opposite and both are defensible. In `git merge feature`, the feature branch is the source and the branch you are on is the target, because the *content* flows that way even though the *pointer* moves the other way. So "source" and "target" are ambiguous here in a way that no amount of care in the message will fix, since each reader arrives with one of the two models already installed.

The tell is the deletion step. Under your labels we would write "delete the destination bookmark", which reads as undoing the thing you just arrived at, when what is actually happening is that the marker is redundant because `main` is now there.

So my suggestion is to stop using source and target altogether and name the two by role, which is unambiguous under either model:

- `<branch>`, the bookmark that advances, typically `main`
- `<cycle>`, the cycle bookmark it advances to, and which is deleted afterwards

That makes the precondition `jj log -r '<branch>::<cycle>'`, which reads in your direction, and it makes the CLI shape `vc-x1 <verb> <cycle>` with `<branch>` coming from config and an override flag, so the two-argument confusion never arises for the common case.

Want me to make that swap through the draft, or keep source and target with your assignment stated explicitly?
